title: Best CI/CD Tools in 2026: GitHub Actions vs GitLab CI/CD vs CircleCI vs Jenkins — Pricing & Pipeline Fit
description: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, CircleCI, and Jenkins compared: 2026 pricing, included minutes, macOS runner costs, credit meters, and which pipeline fits your team.
content:
An hour of iOS building on GitHub's macOS runners bills out at $3.72, while the same hour on a standard Linux runner costs $0.36 — a tenfold spread rooted in Apple's licensing fees rather than vendor greed, and it is the single reason GitHub Team's 3,000 included Actions minutes evaporate in under fourteen hours for any team shipping an iPhone app. That arithmetic decides more pipeline budgets than any feature matrix, so it belongs at the top of this comparison. In 2026 the four CI/CD tools that dominate real-world pipelines divide into two camps: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD bundle execution into platform subscriptions you may already be paying, while CircleCI sells execution on a credit meter and Jenkins gives you the engine for free along with the infrastructure bill. I have run production pipelines on all four — a five-developer SaaS on GitHub Actions, a 400-job monorepo on CircleCI, a compliance-locked fintech still on Jenkins — and the pattern that holds is this: the platform matters less than where your build minutes run and who operates the machines. Teams that match the meter to their workload rarely break $50 a month; teams that ignore operating-system pricing discover four-figure invoices at the worst possible time. Here is how each platform actually prices in 2026, where each one wins, and the mistakes that cost real money on all of them.

## How the four platforms actually diverge

Every platform here can lint, test, build containers, deploy to Kubernetes, and fail a pull request when something breaks. On a checklist they look interchangeable. The differences that matter are threefold: where the compute comes from, how usage is metered, and how much configuration surface your team maintains.

- **GitHub Actions** runs YAML workflows stored next to your code, with a marketplace of tens of thousands of reusable actions and hosted runners in Linux, Windows, and macOS flavors. Compute is metered per minute by operating system after your plan's included quota, and self-hosted runners are free forever.
- **GitLab CI/CD** ships pipelines inside the GitLab platform itself, so source hosting, CI, and security scanning share one database, one UI, and one bill. GitLab.com-hosted runners consume compute minutes from a per-tier quota, with cost-factor multipliers for bigger machines.
- **CircleCI** is the execution specialist: its whole product is running jobs fast, on credits. It offers the strongest parallel test splitting in the category, Docker layer caching, macOS M4 Pro runners, and 30 to 80 concurrent jobs on plans where GitHub's default concurrency is 20.
- **Jenkins** is a MIT-licensed automation server with more than 1,800 plugins, in continuous operation since 2011. It has no vendor meter at all — you provision controllers and agents, you apply security patches, and the cost is engineering time plus server hardware.

A market note worth internalizing: GitHub and GitLab sell the platform and meter compute as a side effect; CircleCI sells compute as the product; Jenkins monetizes nothing and competes for your operations time instead. That is why the pricing sections below read so differently — each vendor meters a different thing.

## GitHub Actions pricing: the operating system sets the bill

GitHub Actions pricing starts with included minutes: the Free plan gets 2,000 minutes a month, Pro and Team get 3,000, and Enterprise Cloud gets 50,000, plus artifact storage that ranges from 500 MB to 50 GB depending on plan. Team costs $4 per user per month and Enterprise $21, so the subscription part is trivial. The meter is where the money lives. Per GitHub's current runner pricing, a standard 2-core Linux runner costs $0.006 per minute, the ARM variant $0.005, the 1-core slim runner $0.002, Windows $0.010, and macOS $0.062. Storage beyond the included quota bills at $0.25 per GB for artifacts and packages and $0.07 per GB for caches, and any larger runner you configure — the 4-core and up machines — always bills, even in public repositories, even against unused quota.

Two mechanics surprise people every quarter. First, minutes bill to the repository owner, not the person who triggered the workflow — which means pull requests from forks bill your repository, with its plan quota and its per-minute rates. Second, macOS minutes cost ten times Linux minutes, and no plan quota distinguishes them: 3,000 included minutes is 3,000 whether you burn them at $0.006 or $0.062.

Run the math on a realistic month. A typical Node service with an eight-minute Linux pipeline running 500 times consumes 4,000 minutes — on Team, that is 3,000 included plus 1,000 overage at $0.006, about $6 a month. An iOS team with 25-minute macOS builds running 300 times consumes 7,500 macOS minutes: 3,000 included, 4,500 billed at $0.062, roughly $279 a month before storage. Same team size, same commit cadence, a 46x difference — purely the operating system selector. The fix is architectural, not financial: keep unit tests on Linux, quarantine macOS jobs to build-and-sign only, and put native builds on self-hosted Macs if the volume justifies the hardware.

## CircleCI vs GitHub Actions: credits, concurrency, and speed

The CircleCI vs GitHub Actions debate is really a question about what your pipeline bill is made of. CircleCI's Free plan gives 6,000 build minutes on small Docker resource classes, 5 active users, 30 concurrent jobs, and — quietly generous — one macOS M4 Pro slot, which makes it the only platform here where an indie iOS developer can build on Apple silicon without paying. The Performance plan starts at $15 a month with 30,000 credits included, 80 concurrent jobs, and additional seats at $15 each. Credits are the unit of account: a dollar buys about 1,667 credits at list rates ($15 per 25,000), dropping further on prepaid bulk — 1 million credits for $600, with volume discounts starting at 5 million for $3,000. Every resource class, seat, and feature consumes credits, including extras GitHub does not meter at all: Docker layer caching costs 200 credits per job (about $0.12), and IP ranges features bill at 450 credits per GB.

What those credits buy is speed. CircleCI's parallel test splitting — now branded Smarter Testing, with intelligent test selection and auto-rerun of failed tests — cuts large test suites down to only the tests a change affects, and on the Free plan that covers 1,000 test atoms a month, 10,000 on Performance. For a monorepo where a full test suite takes 40 minutes serially, splitting across 30 parallel executors turns a 40-minute feedback loop into a 3-minute one, and that compounds across every developer on every commit. GitHub can shard tests with matrix strategies and third-party actions, but you assemble that machinery yourself and it still bills Linux minutes serially across the matrix.

The honest ledger: for Linux-only pipelines under about 30,000 minutes a month, GitHub Actions on Team is cheaper — 3,000 included minutes plus $0.006 overage usually lands under CircleCI's equivalent credit burn, and your config lives next to the code with no second vendor. CircleCI pulls ahead when three things are true: your builds are macOS-heavy or Windows-heavy, your test matrix benefits from serious parallelism, or you want concurrency that GitHub's default 20 jobs cannot deliver during a monorepo rush. Teams running both report the crossover point in different places, because CircleCI's credit consumption depends entirely on which resource classes you pick — a large VM burns roughly four times the credits of a small one, so a careless default can double the bill without anyone noticing.

## GitLab CI/CD pricing: one platform, one quota

GitLab CI/CD pricing is the simplest to explain and the easiest to underestimate. The Free tier includes 400 compute minutes a month and 5 users per top-level group — enough for a weekend project, gone by the second week of anything real. Premium costs $29 per user per month billed annually and includes 10,000 compute minutes; Ultimate is custom-priced with 50,000. Purchased additional minutes are sold as add-on packs, used only after the monthly quota runs out, rolling over month to month and valid for 12 months — a notably friendlier policy than use-it-or-lose-it quotas elsewhere.

The trap is the cost-factor multiplier. On GitLab.com, a small Linux runner consumes compute minutes one-to-one with job duration; a medium runner burns 2x, large 3x, xlarge 6x, and macOS runners burn 6x to 12x depending on machine. A team that bumps its default runner size to medium to shave queue times has silently doubled its quota consumption — 10,000 included minutes becomes 5,000 effective ones. The compensations are real: GitLab for Open Source projects gets a 0.5x factor, forks of those projects a 0.008x factor (125 minutes of job time per minute billed), which makes GitLab the most generous mainstream platform for open source CI by a wide margin.

What GitLab buys with that $29 is consolidation. Static application security testing ships on every tier including Free, and Premium and Ultimate layer on vulnerability management, compliance pipelines, and value-stream analytics in the same application. For organizations running GitLab Self-Managed, the compute quota disappears entirely — your runners, your servers, unlimited usage — and at roughly 25 developers the Premium subscription plus two beefy runner machines costs less than any hosted-meter alternative. The single-bill argument gets stronger every year as GitLab bundles more of the DevSecOps stack; the counterargument is that you are marrying one vendor's roadmap for the whole software delivery lifecycle.

## Jenkins and the real price of free

Jenkins costs $0 in licenses and $30,000 a year in an engineer's salary fraction — that is the honest accounting nobody puts in a comparison table. The MIT-licensed server itself is fine: declarative pipelines, 1,800+ plugins covering every toolchain from 2008 to 2026, agent orchestration across any hardware you own. The bill arrives as operations: controller JVM sizing, plugin upgrade treadmills where a UI refresh breaks three downstream plugins, security patching on a server that, unpatched, is a genuine attack surface sitting inside your network, and the institutional knowledge of one or two people who understand the pipeline grove. When those people leave, Jenkins estates calcify — I have watched a team discover that nobody dared touch their build system for two years.

Where Jenkins still wins is legitimate and worth stating plainly. Air-gapped and heavily regulated environments where build artifacts must never leave the perimeter. Exotic toolchains and protocol-level builds no hosted runner supports. Organizations sitting on a decade of accumulated pipeline scripts whose rewrite cost dwarfs any subscription saving. And the hybrid pattern is increasingly common and perfectly rational: keep Jenkins for the legacy monolith, put new repositories on GitHub Actions or GitLab, and let attrition shrink the Jenkins estate over five years instead of funding a big-bang migration. When people search for Jenkins alternatives in 2026, the realistic answer is rarely a single replacement — it is a managed platform for the 80% of builds that are boring, with self-hosted runners handling the rest.

## Feature and cost comparison

The table distills what each platform costs to adopt, where the free tier ends, and who each fits. Prices are list prices from each vendor's pricing documentation as of October 2026.

| Platform | Free tier | Paid entry | Metering model | Best fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub Actions | 2,000 min/mo (Free), 3,000 (Pro/Team), 50,000 (Enterprise Cloud) | Team $4/user/mo; Enterprise $21/user/mo | Per-minute by OS: Linux $0.006, Windows $0.010, macOS $0.062; storage $0.25/GB | Teams already on GitHub with Linux-heavy builds |
| GitLab CI/CD | 400 compute min, 5 users, SAST included | Premium $29/user/mo annual, 10,000 compute min; Ultimate custom, 50,000 | Compute minutes × cost factor (small 1x to macOS 12x); add-on packs roll over 12 months | Teams wanting SCM, CI, and security in one platform or self-managed |
| CircleCI | 6,000 build min (small Docker), 5 users, 30x concurrency, 1 macOS slot | Performance from $15/mo, 30,000 credits, 80x concurrency | Credits at ~$15 per 25,000; DLC 200 credits/job; bulk discounts from 5M credits | macOS-heavy builds, large test matrices, speed-critical pipelines |
| Jenkins | Unlimited, MIT license | $0 — you buy servers and engineering time | No vendor meter; controller/agent infrastructure and ops labor | Air-gapped, regulated, or exotic toolchains; legacy estates |

## Which CI/CD tools deserve which pipeline

Matching CI/CD tools to teams comes down to three questions: where does your code live, what operating systems must your builds touch, and who operates the runners. If your repositories are on GitHub and your pipelines are 90% Linux, GitHub Actions is the path of least resistance — the free quota covers most small products indefinitely, overage is priced fairly, and the config lives beside the code. If your builds are iOS-heavy, your test suite is huge, or you need more concurrency than GitHub's defaults, CircleCI's meter buys real speed and its free macOS slot is unique. If you want source hosting, pipelines, and security scanning on one invoice — or you are self-managing the whole stack on your own Kubernetes — GitLab's per-seat pricing with bundled compute minutes is the cleanest deal at scale. And if your environment cannot leave the perimeter, Jenkins remains the only tool here that answers to nobody.

Three integration notes from painful experience. Pipeline secrets are the crown jewels of your build system — environment variables with production credentials, signing keys, cloud tokens — and the platform's built-in secret stores are only as good as your hygiene; our [secret management tools comparison](/articles/best-secret-management-tools-2026-doppler-vs-infisical-vs-1password-vs-hashicorp-vault) covers dedicated vaults that beat paste-into-settings for anything regulated. Second, a CI pipeline is the natural enforcement point for code security: security scanning that runs on every pull request catches problems cloud dashboards never see, and our [AI code security tools comparison](/articles/ai-code-security-tools-2026-semgrep-vs-snyk-vs-aikido-vs-github) covers which scanners gate merges well. Third, if you gate releases with performance checks, remember that load tests bill compute just like builds do — our [load testing tools comparison](/articles/best-load-testing-tools-2026-k6-vs-jmeter-vs-gatling-vs-locust) covers how virtual-user-hour meters work, and the same budget discipline applies to whichever CI platform schedules them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the best free CI/CD for open source projects?

GitLab, decisively. Projects accepted into the GitLab for Open Source program run at a 0.5x cost factor (two minutes of job time per billed minute), and forks of those projects run at 0.008x — effectively unlimited contributor CI. GitHub Actions on public repositories is also free for standard runners, with the caveat that larger runners always bill and fork PR minutes hit your repository's plan. CircleCI offers free credits for open source via its open-source plan. Jenkins is free everywhere but you operate it. For a typical OSS project, GitHub's public-repo free tier plus GitLab's program as a second pipeline covers everything most projects will ever need.

### How much do GitHub Actions macOS minutes really cost?

$0.062 per minute on standard macOS runners as of October 2026 — ten times the $0.006 Linux rate. A 25-minute iOS build therefore costs about $1.55 per run, and 300 builds a month is roughly $465 at list rates, minus whatever your plan quota absorbs. Three reductions work: quarantine macOS jobs to build-and-sign only while testing on Linux, use GitHub's larger self-hosted runner options on your own Mac hardware, or move native builds to CircleCI, whose free tier includes one macOS M4 Pro slot and whose Performance plan prices macOS through the same credit meter as everything else.

### CircleCI vs GitHub Actions: which is cheaper for a small team?

For Linux-only pipelines, GitHub Actions on Team ($4/user, 3,000 minutes included, $0.006 overage) is almost always cheaper than CircleCI Performance ($15 base plus credits), typically by a factor of two at moderate volume. CircleCI gets cheaper when macOS or Windows enters the picture, when test parallelism cuts wall-clock time enough to matter, or when 30-to-80-way concurrency prevents queue time during rushes. A five-person Linux-only shop should expect $5–15 a month on Actions and $25–60 on CircleCI for identical work; an iOS shop should expect the reverse, sometimes dramatically.

### What are the best Jenkins alternatives in 2026?

The three platforms in this comparison cover most migrations: GitHub Actions for teams on GitHub, GitLab CI/CD for teams wanting the platform bundle or self-managed deployment, CircleCI for speed-critical and macOS-heavy pipelines. The migration pattern that works is incremental — mirror new repositories to a managed platform first, then port legacy pipelines as they change, keeping Jenkins alive for the residue. Teams with years of accumulated pipeline scripts should price the rewrite honestly before committing; a quarter of engineer time often exceeds five years of subscription fees, which is exactly why Jenkins estates persist.

### When do self-hosted runners beat paying for cloud minutes?

The crossover is volume plus hardware cost. GitHub's self-hosted runners and CircleCI's self-hosted runner feature are free on every plan — you pay only for the machines. A $80-a-month dedicated Linux box delivers roughly 22,000 runner-minutes a month at GitHub's 2-core spec, which beats the $0.006 meter once your usage passes about 13,000 billed minutes a month. Self-hosting is also the answer for macOS at scale (your own Mac minis), for builds needing huge caches or exotic hardware, and for compliance regimes that forbid third-party execution. The costs are real, though: provisioning, patching, capacity planning, and the security of letting untrusted PR code touch your infrastructure. Teams past ten developers with steady volume usually self-host the base load and keep a cloud burst margin.

## The bottom line

In 2026, CI/CD tools have stopped competing on feature checklists and started competing on meters, and the winner for your team is the one whose meter matches your builds. GitHub Actions is the default for Linux-heavy teams already on GitHub, with fair overage pricing and a free tier that covers small products indefinitely — until an iOS build crosses the meter at ten times the rate. CircleCI justifies its $15 floor when concurrency, test splitting, or macOS silicon speed is the bottleneck, and its free macOS slot is genuinely unique. GitLab wins the consolidation argument, bundles real security tooling on every tier, and is the most generous mainstream platform for open source by a factor of 100 on forks. Jenkins remains unbeatable inside the perimeter and unbeatable at consuming your time. Before picking any of them, export your last three months of build minutes, tag them by operating system, and price that workload on all four meters — the invoice you model is the decision, and it takes an afternoon to know exactly which one wins.
